draft.title: Environmental quality and where people live
card: Environmental quality is how clean, healthy and pleasant the natural surroundings of a place are. It is one part of how liveable a place is.
Clean air and water, green space, views and a pleasant climate can draw people to a place. People often like to live near parks, bushland or a beach.
Pollution can push people away. Smoky air, dirty water and rubbish make a place less healthy and less pleasant.
Environmental quality is not the only reason people choose a place. Jobs, cost and family also matter, so people weigh these things up.
draft.remember: Good environmental quality can draw people in. Pollution can push them away.

a.q: Which of these is most likely to draw people to live in a place?
opts: Clean air and plenty of parks
Smoke haze that lasts for weeks
Rivers with rubbish and dirty water
Loud noise from a rubbish tip nearby
a.why: Clean air and green space make a place healthier and more pleasant, so they can draw people in. The other options are forms of pollution, which can push people away.
a.clue: Think about which choice makes a place healthier and more pleasant.

b.q: Tom lives in a town in Western Australia where dust from a nearby mine often fills the air. His family is thinking of moving. Which reason fits this idea best?
opts: Pollution can push people away from a place
Pollution always forces people to leave a town
Dust makes a town's climate more pleasant
Mines give a town better environmental quality
b.why: Dust in the air is a form of pollution, and pollution can push people away from a place. It does not always force people to leave, because jobs and family may keep them there.
b.clue: Pollution is a push factor, but the card says it only can push.

a.best: Clean air and plenty of parks

b.best: Pollution can push people away from a place

problems.detail: The clue gives the answer away. It tells students the card says pollution 'can push', which points straight to the only option with that wording. It also uses 'push factor', a term the card never teaches.

The clue says the card 'only can push', using 'only' where the card says 'can'. The distractor 'Pollution always forces people to leave a town' also uses 'always' and 'forces'. It is meant to be wrong, but it should still be flagged under the absolute-wording rule.
The stem 'Which reason fits this idea best?' is vague. It does not say what 'this idea' is, for example why Tom's family might want to move.

check.summary: The card, remember line and question a are sound. Question b's clue gives the answer away and uses 'only' and 'push factor', and its stem ('this idea') is vague and should be reworded.

b.q: Tom lives in a Western Australian town where dust from a nearby mine often fills the air. His dad works at the mine. His family is unsure whether to move. Which reason best explains why?
opts: Dust can push them away, but the job may keep them
Dust can draw them in, but the job may push them away
Dust does not affect where a family chooses to live
Dust improves the air quality, so they want to stay
b.why: Dusty air is pollution, which can push people away. The job is a different reason that may keep them there, so the family weighs the two up. Saying the dust draws them in reverses its effect, because pollution makes a place less healthy and less pleasant.
b.clue: Think about what the dust and the job each do for the family.
